results.result: Human participants achieved 77.94% accuracy on the reading comprehension task, while simple heuristic models (orthographic: 25.6%, semantic: 27.3%) and the SAR model (47.6%) performed poorly. Transformer-based models achieved 37.08% accuracy after pre-training and 73% after fine-tuning, approaching human performance.
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C21 provide converging evidence from human behavioral data and computational model performance. The low accuracy of simple models (C17-C19) demonstrates task complexity, while transformer models' improvement with fine-tuning (C21) shows they can approach human-level performance (C16). All claims are supported by data presented in Figure 1B.

results.result: Participants in Experiment 1 read passages at 457±142 words/min, approximately twice the normal reading speed for native readers, indicating development of a specialized reading strategy for the goal-directed task.
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C24 are well-supported by experimental data (C22, C23) and comparison to established reading norms (C24). The inference that faster reading indicates a specialized strategy is reasonable given the task demands and is supported by Figure 1C data.

results.result: Transformer-based DNN attention weights predict human word reading time better than heuristic models or SAR. Predictive power increased from ~0.2 (heuristic models) to ~0.3 (random transformers) to ~0.5 (pre-trained transformers), with fine-tuning further boosting prediction for local but not global questions.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C29 present a clear progression of model performance supported by correlation analyses and statistical testing (Figure 3A, Supplementary file 1a). The differential effect of fine-tuning on local vs. global questions (C29) is particularly well-documented and adds specificity to the findings.

results.result: Layout and word features significantly predict word reading time, with layout features showing stronger effects for global than local questions. However, transformer-based model attention weights provide superior predictive power compared to these basic text features alone.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C34 are supported by regression analyses (Figure 3B, Supplementary file 1b) and linear mixed effects modeling (C33). The statistical comparisons (C31, C34) demonstrate both the contribution of text features and the additional explanatory power of DNN attention weights.

results.result: After controlling for layout, word features, and question relevance, transformer-based model attention weights still significantly predict residual word reading time (predictive power ~0.2-0.3), with more than 85% of DNN attention heads contributing to predictions.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C38 demonstrate that DNN attention captures information beyond basic text and task features through systematic regression analyses (Figure 3—figure supplements 1B-C). The linear mixed effects model result (C38) provides additional statistical rigor, though the drop in predictive power suggests substantial overlap with measured features.

results.result: Question-relevant words show distinct spatial distributions: uniformly distributed for local questions but concentrated at passage beginnings for global questions. Readers allocate more reading time to passage beginnings for global questions and to lines with highest question relevance.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C43 are well-supported by annotation data (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A-B) and eye-tracking analyses (Figure 3C-D). The convergence between question relevance annotations and actual reading behavior strengthens the validity of both measures.

results.result: Human attention shows temporal dynamics: layout features increasingly influence late reading stages for global questions, word features remain stable across stages, while question relevance effects increase from early (gaze duration) to late (rereading) stages, suggesting hierarchical attention control.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C47 are supported by analysis of different eye-tracking measures (Figure 4A, Supplementary file 1d). The inference about hierarchical control (C47) is reasonable given the temporal progression of effects, though alternative explanations are not explicitly ruled out.

results.result: DNN attention weights show layer-specific sensitivity: shallow layers are sensitive to word features across all model types, while deep layers are sensitive to question relevance only in fine-tuned models, indicating that goal-directed attention emerges through task-specific training.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C50 are supported by layer-wise regression analyses (Figure 4B-C, Figure 4—figure supplements 2-3). The parallel between human temporal dynamics and DNN layer hierarchy strengthens the computational account, though the inference about training-induced goal-directed attention (C50) could benefit from additional mechanistic evidence.

results.result: Experiment 2 (mixed question types) showed slower reading (298±123 words/min) than Experiment 1 (blocked design), with reduced question-type-specific effects. Fine-tuned models better predicted reading time than pre-trained models, but task modulation effects were weaker than in Experiment 1, indicating that blocked presentation facilitated development of question-type-specific strategies.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C59 are well-supported by systematic comparisons between Experiments 1 and 2 (Figure 5A-D, Figure 5—figure supplements 1-2). The inference about strategy development (C59) is reasonable given the convergent evidence from reading speed, model predictions, and attention effects, though the specific mechanisms remain unspecified.

results.result: Native readers (Experiment 3) read faster (506±155 words/min) than L2 readers (Experiment 2) with comparable accuracy. Task modulation of reading time was significant but weaker for native readers, with layout effects dominating gaze duration and word/task features dominating rereading.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C70 are supported by comprehensive comparisons between Experiments 2 and 3 (Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplements 1B-2B). The differential processing patterns between native and L2 readers are well-documented, though the interpretation about processing efficiency (C70) involves some speculation about underlying mechanisms.

results.result: During general-purpose reading without a question (Experiment 4), reading speed was slower (225±40 words/min) than goal-directed reading. Pre-trained and fine-tuned models showed similar predictive power, word reading time was predicted by layout and word features but not question relevance, and question-type-specific effects were absent, confirming task-dependence of goal-directed attention.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C78 provide strong evidence for task-dependent attention through systematic comparison with Experiments 1-3 (Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplements 1C-2B). The absence of question relevance effects (C74, C77) and question-type differences (C76) in the control condition validates the task-specific nature of effects observed in goal-directed reading.

results.result: Human attention distribution during goal-directed reading is explained by task-optimized transformer DNN attention weights, while general-purpose reading is explained by word-prediction-optimized models. Text features modulate first-pass reading while question relevance modulates rereading, especially for L2 readers.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C82 synthesize the main findings across all experiments. These summary claims are well-supported by the extensive empirical evidence from model comparisons, eye-tracking analyses, and cross-experiment comparisons, though they represent high-level interpretations of the data.

results.result: In DNNs, basic text features modulate attention weights in shallow layers while question relevance modulates deep layers, with both contributing to prediction of human reading time, reflecting hierarchical attention control for task optimization.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C85 are supported by layer-wise regression analyses (Figure 4B, Figure 3—figure supplement 2). The parallel between DNN layer hierarchy and human temporal processing stages provides computational support for hierarchical attention control, though the mechanistic correspondence requires careful interpretation.

results.result: Pre-training on word prediction tasks produces text-based attention explaining general-purpose reading (Experiment 4), while fine-tuning on reading comprehension produces goal-directed attention explaining task-specific reading (Experiments 1-3).
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C87 are supported by systematic model comparisons across experiments (Figures 4B and 5A). The differential predictive power of pre-trained vs. fine-tuned models across task conditions provides strong evidence for training-induced attention specialization.

results.result: Pre-training on word prediction tasks enables models to learn statistical regularities including word surprisal, which modulates human reading time. Tokenization processes also contribute to similarity between human and DNN attention by allocating more attention to longer words.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C94 provide mechanistic explanations for DNN-human correspondence, supported by citations to model development literature (C88-C89), reading research (C91), and neuroscience (C92). The explanations about surprisal (C90) and tokenization (C93-C94) are reasonable inferences about model properties, though direct empirical validation in this study is limited.

results.result: Previous reading models (E-Z reader, SWIFT) predict eye movements based on text features and optimization principles. Recent work showed RNN models can capture goal-directed attention for simple word-matching tasks, but the current study demonstrates that transformer models better capture attention for complex questions requiring inference.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C100 accurately characterize prior work (supported by citations C95-C98) and position the current findings (C99-C100, supported by Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1). The comparison to prior models is appropriate and well-documented.

results.result: Previous studies showed inconsistent results about whether readers spend more time on task-relevant information, potentially due to working memory and topic familiarity. The current study confirms that L2 readers spend more time on question-relevant information than native readers, possibly because skilled readers process efficiently without extra encoding time.
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C103 are supported by citations and experimental data (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 2B). However, C104 is explicitly speculative about mechanisms ("it is possible that"), and alternative explanations for native-L2 differences (e.g., covert attention, different strategies) are not empirically tested in this study.

results.result: Previous studies showed mixed results about DNN attention interpretability and correlation with human reading time. The current results suggest this inconsistency may arise because deep layers are tuned to task relevance (which weakly affects native readers) while shallow layers capture text features (which reliably affect all readers).
results.evaluation: Claims C105-C109 accurately characterize conflicting prior findings (supported by citations). Claims C110-C113 provide a coherent explanation based on the current study's layer-wise analyses and native-L2 comparisons. The explanation is reasonable but represents a post-hoc interpretation that would benefit from direct testing.

results.result: Task-optimized transformer models automatically generate human-like attention without prior knowledge of human reading processes. Simpler models that fail at the task also fail to predict attention. The dataset and methods provide a probe for testing biological plausibility of NLP models, though human-like attention may not be a unique solution.
results.evaluation: Claims C114-C115 are well-supported by the systematic model comparisons throughout the study. Claims C116-C118 acknowledge limitations and broader implications appropriately. C116 is explicitly speculative but reasonable, while C117-C118 discuss methodological contributions that are supported by the demonstrated utility of the approach.

results.result: The study used 800 question/passage pairs from the RACE dataset, with six question types (three local, three global) that could not be answered by simple word matching. Participants were high-proficiency L2 readers (Experiments 1-2, 4) or native readers (Experiment 3) who were confident about their answers (90.47% confident, mean rating 3.25/4).
results.evaluation: Claims C119-C124 describe the experimental materials and participants, supported by data presentation and participant screening criteria. The confidence ratings (C123-C124) validate that participants were engaged and capable of performing the task, supporting the validity of the behavioral data.

results.result: The study demonstrates that participants achieved 77.94% accuracy on reading comprehension questions, while simple heuristic models (orthographic: 25.6%, semantic: 27.3%) and RNN-based models (SAR: 47.6%) performed poorly. Transformer-based models achieved 37.08% after pre-training and 73% after fine-tuning, approaching human performance.
results.evaluation: All reviewers acknowledge the task performance results without critique. Reviewer 1 states the evidence is 'convincing,' and Reviewer 2 notes the models 'show a statistically reliable fit to these reading patterns above-and-beyond text- and semantic-similarity baseline metrics.' The comparison across model types is treated as methodologically sound.

results.result: Participants in Experiment 1 read passages at 457±142 words/min, almost twice the normal reading speed for native readers, indicating a specialized reading strategy for the goal-directed task.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these behavioral findings without question. The fast reading speed is implicitly acknowledged as part of the task-directed behavior that the study investigates. No concerns are raised about this measurement or its interpretation.

results.result: Transformer-based DNN attention weights predict human word reading time significantly better than heuristic models and RNN models. Pre-trained transformers achieved ~0.5 predictive power, fine-tuned models reached higher values for local questions, and predictions remained significant even after controlling for text features and question relevance.
results.evaluation: Reviewers consistently affirm this core finding. Reviewer 1 states 'attention-weights from a deep neural network show a statistically reliable fit to the word-level reading patterns,' and Reviewer 2 notes 'statistically reliable fit...above-and-beyond text- and semantic-similarity baseline metrics.' The hierarchical analysis controlling for covariates is accepted without critique.

results.result: Layout features, word features, and question relevance all significantly predict word reading time. Layout features showed stronger effects for global than local questions, and question relevance remained significant even after controlling for text features.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these text/task feature analyses as supporting evidence. Reviewer 3 specifically notes 'the modeling uses text- and question-based features in addition to DNNs, specifically evaluates relevant effects' as a strength. The regression analyses are treated as methodologically appropriate.

results.result: Question-relevant words were uniformly distributed for local questions but concentrated at passage beginnings for global questions. Eye-tracking data confirmed readers spent more time on passage beginnings for global questions and on lines with highest question relevance.
results.evaluation: These findings about spatial distribution of attention are accepted by reviewers as part of the evidence for task-directed reading. Reviewer 3 notes the study 'directly modeling the question relevance of each word' as strengthening the conclusions. No concerns are raised about these analyses.

results.result: Layout features influenced early reading stages for global questions, word features remained stable across stages, while question relevance effects increased from early to late reading stages, suggesting text-based attention develops early while task influence emerges later.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the temporal dynamics analysis. The distinction between early and late processing stages aligns with the hierarchical attention framework that reviewers find convincing. No methodological concerns are raised about the gaze duration vs. rereading analysis.

results.result: Layer-wise analysis revealed that shallow DNN layers are sensitive to word features across all model types, while deep layers become sensitive to question relevance only in fine-tuned models, demonstrating hierarchical evolution of text-based and goal-directed attention.
results.evaluation: Reviewers treat this hierarchical layer analysis as a key contribution. Reviewer 3 notes 'compares vanilla pretrained and task-finetuned models' as making 'results more transparent and helps assess the contributions of task optimization.' The layer-wise decomposition is accepted as valid evidence for the optimization hypothesis.

results.result: Experiment 2 (mixed question types) showed slower reading (298±123 words/min) than Experiment 1 (blocked), with higher predictive power for layout/word features but lower for question relevance, indicating that readers developed question-type-specific strategies in the blocked design.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 4 explicitly identifies this as a weakness: 'Experiment 1 tests questions from different types in blocks...the paper provides evidence that this encourages the development of question-type-specific reading strategies...On the other hand, finetuning the model on one of the two types does not seem to reproduce this differential behavior.' This represents a limitation in the model's ability to capture human adaptive behavior.

results.result: Experiment 3 with native English speakers showed faster reading (506±155 words/min) than L2 readers, with weaker task modulation effects. Native readers showed significant but reduced question relevance effects compared to L2 readers, suggesting more efficient processing.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the L1 vs. L2 comparison as strengthening the study. Reviewer 3 lists 'conducts experiments on both L2 and L1 speakers' as a strength. The interpretation that native readers show weaker overt attention effects is consistent with the efficiency explanation that reviewers do not challenge.

results.result: Experiment 4 (passage preview without question) showed slowest reading (225±40 words/min), with pre-trained and fine-tuned models performing similarly. Question relevance did not predict reading time, confirming task-dependence of goal-directed attention effects.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm this control experiment. Reviewer 3 states the claim 'rests on (i) a role of question relevance in influencing reading in Expts 1-2 but not 4, and (ii) the fact that fine-tuned DNNs improve prediction of gaze in Expts 1-2 but not 4.' This experimental contrast is treated as strong evidence for task optimization.

results.result: The study demonstrates that task-optimized transformer-based DNNs can explain human attention distribution in goal-directed reading without prior knowledge of human reading processes, and that simpler models failing to match human performance also fail to predict attention patterns.
results.evaluation: This main theoretical claim is strongly endorsed by reviewers. Reviewer 1 states the work 'strengthens a line of research arguing that attention in reading reflects task optimization.' Reviewer 4 notes 'modeling results contribute to theoretical understanding of human reading behavior, and strengthens a line of research arguing that it reflects task-adaptive behavior.' The evidence is deemed convincing for the optimization hypothesis.

results.result: Pre-training on word prediction tasks introduces sensitivity to word surprisal and text features through learning statistical regularities, which aligns with established findings that word predictability modulates reading time and that pre-trained DNN representations converge with cortical language responses.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this mechanistic explanation for why pre-trained models capture human reading patterns. The connection to surprisal and prior neuroscience findings is treated as appropriate contextualization. No concerns are raised about this interpretive framework.

results.result: The study situates its findings within prior reading research showing effects of word length, frequency, predictability, and line position, as well as previous models (E-Z reader, SWIFT) and mixed findings about task-relevance effects that may depend on working memory and topic familiarity.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this literature contextualization. Reviewer 3 notes 'the claim that human attention reflects optimal behavior is not new, the paper considers a substantially more high-level task in comparison to prior work' as appropriate framing. The review of prior inconsistent findings is not challenged.

results.result: The study addresses mixed prior findings about DNN attention interpretability by showing that last-layer attention is tuned to task-relevant information, but this effect is weak for native readers, potentially explaining inconsistent correlations in prior literature. Shallower layers reliably model text features for all readers.
results.evaluation: Reviewers treat this as a valuable contribution to understanding DNN interpretability. The explanation for prior inconsistencies based on reader proficiency and layer depth is accepted as plausible. No concerns are raised about this reconciliation of prior mixed findings.

results.result: Recent DNN models with attention mechanisms approach or surpass human performance on goal-directed reading tasks, and task-optimized DNNs explain neural response properties across visual and language processing domains.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this as established background. Reviewer 1 notes the work is 'methodologically well grounded in the NLP literature,' and Reviewer 3 states 'the paper leverages recent models from the NLP literature which are known to provide strong performance on such question-answering tasks.' This framing is uncontested.

results.result: The authors speculate that skilled readers may rely on covert attention for efficient processing, acknowledge that different algorithms might solve the same task, and propose their dataset as a probe for testing biological plausibility of NLP models.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these as appropriate interpretive caveats and future directions. Reviewer 4 notes 'the data are likely to be useful as a benchmark in further modeling of eye-movements, an area of interest to computational research on psycholinguistics.' The speculative nature is appropriately qualified.

results.result: The study used 800 question/passage pairs from RACE dataset with six question types (local and global), where questions did not directly appear in passages. Participants were high-proficiency L2 readers who showed 90.47% confidence and 3.25/4 mean confidence ratings.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirm the methodological rigor. Reviewer 2 specifically praises 'stimuli consisting of paragraphs read by middle and high school students, covering a wide range of diverse topics' for enhancing 'ecological validity.' The task design is treated as appropriate for testing the optimization hypothesis.

comparisons.comparison: Perfect agreement on claims C16-C21 regarding task performance and model accuracy. Both evaluations find the evidence convincing and well-supported by Figure 1B data. OpenEval and peer reviewers agree that transformer models approach human-level performance with fine-tuning.

Complete agreement on claims C22-C24 about reading speed and specialized strategies. Both evaluations accept the behavioral findings without critique, treating the fast reading speed as valid evidence of task-directed behavior.

Strong agreement on claims C25-C29 regarding model performance progression. Peer review R3 additionally covers claims C34-C35, C37-C38 from OpenEval R4-R5, affirming the core finding that DNN attention weights fit reading patterns above baseline metrics. Both find the statistical analyses convincing.

Agreement on claims C30-C33 regarding text/task feature regression analyses. Peer review also includes C36 from OpenEval R5. Both evaluations accept the hierarchical modeling approach as methodologically sound, with peer reviewers specifically noting the strength of controlling for text- and question-based features.

OpenEval R5 addresses claims C35-C38 about DNN attention capturing information beyond basic features. Peer R3 covers overlapping claims (C35, C37, C38) as part of broader affirmation of the core DNN-human correspondence finding. Both accept the regression analyses controlling for covariates.

Perfect agreement on claims C39-C43 regarding spatial distribution of attention and question relevance. Both evaluations accept the convergence between annotations and eye-tracking as strengthening the validity of measures. Peer reviewers specifically note direct modeling of question relevance as a strength.

Complete agreement on claims C44-C47 about temporal dynamics and hierarchical control. Both evaluations accept the distinction between early and late processing stages. OpenEval notes alternative explanations aren't ruled out, but peer reviewers raise no methodological concerns.

Agreement on claims C48-C50 regarding layer-wise analyses and temporal-hierarchical parallels. Peer R7 also covers C83-C85 from OpenEval R13. Both treat the hierarchical layer analysis as a key contribution, with peer reviewers noting it makes results more transparent and helps assess task optimization contributions.

Divergence on claims C51-C59 regarding strategy development across question types. OpenEval finds evidence supported, but Peer R8 rates as UNCERTAIN, explicitly noting that fine-tuned models fail to reproduce the differential behavior humans show for different question types in blocked presentation.

Strong agreement on claims C60-C70 regarding L1 vs. L2 reader differences. Peer R9 also includes C103. Both evaluations accept the native-L2 comparison as strengthening the study, with peer reviewers listing it as a specific strength. The efficiency interpretation is not challenged.

Agreement on claims C71-C78 regarding task-dependent attention in control experiment. Peer R10 also covers C80, C86 from other OpenEval results. Both evaluations strongly affirm this control experiment as evidence for task optimization, with peer reviewers explicitly stating it provides strong evidence.

Strong agreement on claims C79-C82 synthesizing main findings. Peer R11 also covers C87, C99-C100, C114-C115 from other OpenEval results. Both evaluations strongly endorse the task optimization hypothesis, with peer reviewers stating the work strengthens this line of research and contributes to theoretical understanding.

Agreement on claims C83-C85 regarding hierarchical layer analysis and temporal processing parallels. Peer R7 groups these with C48-C50 from OpenEval R8. Both accept the layer-wise decomposition as valid evidence for the optimization hypothesis and hierarchical attention control.

Agreement on claims C86-C87 regarding differential predictive power of pre-trained vs. fine-tuned models. Peer R10 groups C86 with control experiment findings. Both evaluations accept this as strong evidence for training-induced attention specialization across task conditions.

Perfect agreement on claims C88-C94 regarding mechanistic explanations for DNN-human correspondence. Both evaluations accept the connection to surprisal and neuroscience findings as appropriate contextualization. Peer reviewers note the work is methodologically well grounded in NLP literature.
